title: Local determination of low-energy states in gapped fermion systems with weak long-range interactions
abstract: We consider bulk-gapped fermion systems whose infinite-volume bulk is obtained by adding sufficiently weak even many-body interactions to a free Hamiltonian with spectral gap $g>0$, allowing polynomial spatial decay of both parts. We prove quantitative local determination of low-energy states: whenever another interaction agrees with the bulk interaction inside a finite or infinite region $U$, with bulk terms crossing its boundary unchanged or removed, all its states with excitation energies in $[0,3g/4]$ have local expectations close to those of the bulk ground state deep inside $U$. The error decays with the distance to the complement of $U$, independently of the interaction terms supported outside $U$ and of the chosen low-energy state.   Quantitative local determination has strong consequences. (i) The bulk interaction has a unique algebraic ground state. (ii) A strong "local perturbations perturb locally" (LPPL) principle holds: arbitrary distant defects change local ground-state expectations only by a spatially decaying error. (iii) Low-energy excitations in finite samples remain localized near the boundary for all times, up to spatially decaying tails, uniformly over arbitrary even boundary terms. (iv) Correlations from deep inside $U$ to outside $U$ are small, with quantitative bounds in terms of spatial separation and distance to $U^c$.   To prove local determination of low-energy states, we combine quasi-adiabatic transport of the free ground state to the interacting bulk ground state with a new condition, local excitation detectability (LED). A companion paper establishes gap stability and constructs the transport for weak interactions, while we prove LED at sufficiently weak coupling. The abstract theorem is nonperturbative and applies whenever the transport and LED hypotheses hold.
summary: This theoretical paper proves that in gapped fermion systems with weak long-range interactions, the low-energy physics deep inside a region $U$ is robustly determined by the bulk Hamiltonian, even if the interactions outside $U$ are modified. The key result is a quantitative bound showing that local observables decay away from the boundary. This confirms a strong 'local perturbations perturb locally' principle for these quantum systems.
main_problem: The paper aims to prove the quantitative local determination of low-energy states in gapped fermion systems subjected to weak, long-range interactions.
main_result: It establishes that local expectations of low-energy states deep inside a region $U$ are close to the bulk ground state, with the error decaying with the distance to the boundary of $U$, independent of external perturbations.
method: The proof combines quasi-adiabatic spectral flow techniques with a newly introduced condition called Local Excitation Detectability (LED).
model_or_system: The system consists of bulk-gapped fermion systems defined on a countable metric space, perturbed by weak, even many-body interactions added to a free Hamiltonian with a spectral gap $g>0$.
key_observables: Local expectations of low-energy states (excitation energies in $[0, 3g/4]$) and the decay rate of the error in these expectations.
important_parameters:
The spectral gap $g>0$, the strength of the weak interactions, and the spatial decay rates of the interactions (e.g., polynomial decay $
u$).
main_assumptions: The validity of ground-state transport and the Local Excitation Detectability (LED) hypothesis are crucial assumptions for the main theorem.
paper_structure: The argument develops by first establishing the necessary spectral flow and locality properties (Sections 2, 4, 5, 6) before presenting the main quantitative comparison theorem (Theorem 3.1) and proving the uniqueness of the ground state (Corollary 3.2).
why_interesting: The rigorous mathematical control over local physics in gapped systems, especially the quantitative nature of the error bounds, is highly relevant for understanding thermalization and boundary effects in quantum many-body systems.
